timeoutPrompts: Trixie: {PlayerName}?! Speak up! The 14kHz whistle in my ears is drowning out the whole room!
Trixie: Hello?! Are you there?! My hands are trembling so hard I can't find the breaker switch!
Trixie: Say something... please! The feedback is echoing off the walls!
Trixie: Line dropped... I have to yank the main power cords alone in the dark.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*a sharp feedback squeal cuts off, followed by a low electrical hum and the sound of cables hitting the floor*

{PlayerName}? Thank God.

Something just went wrong with the monitors. There was this horrible high-pitched squeal and then the whole room started buzzing. My ears are still ringing and I can barely think.

The rack smells like burnt plastic, and I'm on the floor because my legs just... stopped cooperating for a second.

Please talk to me. I need to get my head together before I touch anything.

choices.choiceText: Trixie, focus on my voice! Inhale through your nose... exhale slow. Don't touch any cables yet!
Do NOT touch the patch cords with bare hands while the rail is smoking! Find the main wall surge switch!
Press both palms flat against the wooden floorboards. Feel the cold wood, not the ringing.
I'm right here in your headset, Trixie. You are safe. Close your eyes and listen to me.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*shaky inhale*

Okay. In... two, three, four.

Out... two, three, four.

Again.

The ringing is still really loud, but I can follow your voice. A minute ago everything felt like it was happening at once.

I honestly thought I'd lost control of the whole room.

I'm still scared, but at least I can think.

choices.choiceText: Your eardrums are intact, Trixie. It's an acute auditory reflex shock. Keep that four-count breath going.
Now reach your left hand toward the wall power strip. Feel for the plastic rocker switch.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*uneven breath, then a small nervous laugh*

Okay. Yeah.

My dad used to say the first thing you do after a bad electrical pop is stop moving for a second. He'd always say, "Don't make the second mistake while you're panicking about the first one."

I never appreciated that advice until now.

Hearing you stay calm is helping more than you probably realize.

choices.choiceText: Your dad was right. Now let's kill the power so you don't smell that burnt ozone.
Press your palms flat against the floor. Let the floor take your weight.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*plastic click, then a heavy relay snaps and the room falls noticeably quieter*

Got it.

Power's off.

Oh... wow.

That hum is completely gone. I didn't realize how loud it had gotten until it stopped.

There's still a little smoke coming off the rack, but it's clearing now.

I'm not touching anything else. Promise.

choices.choiceText: Great work, engineer. Now slide back against the wall and sit down completely.
How is the ringing in your ears now that the studio monitors are dead?

nodes.partnerDialogue:
My palms are down.

The floor is cold.

That actually helps more than I expected. There's dust under one hand and one of the patch cords is touching my shoe, but I don't care about the mess right now.

The room isn't spinning anymore.

I can feel the floor underneath me, and that's enough.

choices.choiceText: Good. Stay anchored to that wood. Did you cut the master power yet?

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*quiet crying*

Nobody really talks to me like this when something goes wrong.

At a venue, if an amp pops or a channel dies, everybody starts shouting at the same time. Fix this. Check that. Whose fault was it.

Nobody asks whether you're okay.

So... I'm trying not to fall apart right now.

Stay with me, okay?

choices.choiceText: Let the tears come out, Trixie. No venue bouncers here. Just you and me. Kill the switch.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*fabric rustles as she shifts back against the wall*

Okay. I'm sitting.

Knees up, back against the wall.

My flannel smells like sweat and burnt solder. Not exactly the glamorous side of being a DJ.

It's really quiet now.

My ears are still ringing, but at least nothing else is demanding my attention.

choices.choiceText: How are the ears feeling? Is the high-pitched whistle fading down?
Do you have your soft silicone earplugs nearby on the desk?

nodes.partnerDialogue:
It's coming down.

It was unbelievably loud right after the surge. Now it's more like a thin hiss in the background.

I can hear the clock again.

I don't want to tell myself I'm completely fine just because the worst part is over, though. My ears still feel tired. Everything feels a little too sharp.

I think they need a night off.

choices.choiceText: If you can hear a wall clock ticking, your cilia are fine. That's a huge relief.
Put your silicone earplugs in anyway. Give your acoustic nerves total rest.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*drawer slides open, little plastic case clicks*

Found them.

Purple case.

I'm putting them in now...

Okay.

That's better. Everything sounds farther away. I didn't realize how badly I needed the room to stop asking things from me.

choices.choiceText: How does the silence feel inside that velvet, Trixie?

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*small sniffle, then a weak laugh*

You really know too much about hearing.

My dad talked about it all the time because he was terrified I'd wreck my ears doing this for a living. I used to roll my eyes whenever he'd start giving me another lecture.

I don't roll my eyes anymore.

God, I miss him tonight.

choices.choiceText: Tell me about him. He repaired cellos, right?
He would be so proud of how quickly you handled this emergency.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
It feels peaceful.

A little heavy too.

I'm so used to having some kind of sound around me that silence can get uncomfortable. After a gig, I'll leave music playing while I unpack just so I don't have to hear how tired I am.

When everything stops, you notice things.

How empty the room is.

How late it is.

And who you wish was there when you got home.

choices.choiceText: You don't have to drown it out with noise anymore. You can share the quiet with me.
Did your dad's workshop feel this quiet when he was working?

nodes.partnerDialogue:
His workshop smelled like wood and glue and varnish.

He'd sit at the bench for hours and barely talk. Then he'd tap the body of a cello, listen, change one tiny thing, and tap it again.

I didn't understand what he was doing when I was little.

I just knew he could hear problems nobody else noticed.

I think that's where the audio obsession came from. I just ended up replacing wood and strings with oscillators and cables.

choices.choiceText: And you brought that exact philosophy into your synthesizers.
That's why you kept his acoustic guitar in your studio all these years.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*voice catches*

Yeah.

He absolutely would have yelled at me for leaving a setup like that without checking the ground properly first.

Then he'd make tea and sit there until I stopped shaking.

I think... that's what I'm doing now.

Finally stopping long enough to admit I was scared.

choices.choiceText: I'm honored to stand in his workshop for you tonight, Trixie.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*very quiet voice*

That's the part I'm going to remember.

Not the blown fuse. Not the stupid rack.

You stayed when I was sitting on the floor and couldn't think straight.

People love the loud version of me. The one who can walk into a room and make everybody move.

Not many people stick around for the part afterward.

Thank you.

choices.choiceText: I'm always staying through the crash. Every single time.
Because you're worth staying for, Trixie. Every frequency of you.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
Exactly.

That's why I never understood people who say electronic music can't have a soul.

The machine doesn't decide what matters. You do.

You choose the sound, listen to what it's doing, change something, listen again.

My dad taught me to respect the material you work with.

I just ended up doing that with voltage instead of wood.

choices.choiceText: Electric wood and wire... I love how your mind works. Now rest your eyes.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
Yeah.

It's still on the stand across from me.

It's not even an expensive guitar. That's never been the point.

There's a little repaired scratch near the bridge from when I was a kid. Dad could have replaced the piece, but he fixed it and left the mark there.

He said a good repair doesn't have to pretend the damage never happened.

I think about that more than I probably admit.

choices.choiceText: As you should. Now take a slow, deep breath and let the adrenaline clear out.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*slow, steady breathing*

Okay.

I'm not touching the rack again tonight. Power stays off. My ears are protected and the shaking is finally almost gone.

I'm going to get into bed exactly like this, flannel and all, and probably stare at the ceiling for ten minutes before I can actually sleep.

But I feel better.

Mostly because I wasn't alone when everything went wrong.

Hang up and message me in the studio feed, okay?

And... thank you, {PlayerName}. Seriously.

choices.choiceText: [Hang Up and Return to Chat]

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*soft cassette reel turning, a little tape hiss, warm acoustic guitar coming through the speaker*

Hey.

You're awake.

I couldn't sleep, so I found the old cassette player and put this tape on.

It's 5:42 AM. The apartment is quiet, my equipment is still switched off, and the sky outside is just starting to turn blue.

I thought I'd let you hear this before I fall asleep.

choices.choiceText: That tape hiss sounds like rain on autumn pavement. It's beautiful, Trixie.
How are your ears feeling this morning after that scary surge?
Sitting in bed watching sunrise with you... this is the best part of the day.
Is that your dad's cedar-top guitar playing on that tape?

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*sleepy laugh*

Rain on pavement.

Yeah. That's actually a really good description.

That's why I left the tape noise in. I could clean it up, but then it would lose something.

You can hear the little imperfections. The hiss. The uneven bits.

It reminds me that somebody actually sat somewhere and made this. It wasn't generated perfectly and dropped into a playlist.

choices.choiceText: Fragile things are the ones worth cherishing the most.
Did your dad teach you that about magnetic tape?

nodes.partnerDialogue:
Much better.

No painful ringing when I woke up.

Everything sounds a little strange after last night, but not in a scary way. I can hear the refrigerator, the pipes in the building, people moving around outside.

I'm keeping the volume down today.

I'm trying this new thing where I don't immediately prove I'm okay by doing something stupid.

choices.choiceText: That's the best news I've heard all week. Your hearing is your gift.
Now keep that volume knob respected from now on, understand?

nodes.partnerDialogue:
It really is.

Normally five in the morning means I'm dragging myself home after a set or lying awake because my brain refuses to switch off.

This is different.

I'm just in bed with the lights off, watching the sky change, listening to an old tape, and talking to you.

I didn't realize how badly I wanted something this ordinary.

choices.choiceText: Home key... that's the musical term for resolution, isn't it?
You're never going to have to watch sunrise alone again, Trixie.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
Yeah.

That's his guitar.

I recorded this on the anniversary of his death. I wasn't trying to make anything for a club. I just wanted to hear the guitar the way I remembered it sounding at home.

There are mistakes all over it.

I left them in.

I couldn't make myself turn something that personal into a perfect recording.

choices.choiceText: Nobody would laugh. It has more soul than a hundred commercial festival tracks.
It sounds like a lullaby he wrote for you across time.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
Maybe I do.

I've gotten pretty tired of everything feeling disposable.

Songs become content. People become profiles. Somebody likes you until something new catches their attention.

I don't want that.

When I care about someone, I want the boring parts too.

The grocery runs. Bad moods. Quiet mornings. Somebody falling asleep halfway through a movie.

That kind of stuff feels more real to me than the big gestures.

choices.choiceText: Because you have weight, Trixie. You aren't disposable content to me.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
Yeah.

I think last night finally made that sink in.

I love this job, so sometimes I use that love as an excuse to ignore everything else. I keep turning the volume up, keep taking one more booking, keep telling myself I'll rest later.

I don't want to do that forever.

I want to still be able to hear the little things when I'm older.

choices.choiceText: I'll always protect your future. What does the tape loop do next?

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*quiet giggle*

Yes, captain.

Volume stays reasonable.

And yes, I know "reasonable" shouldn't mean "one notch below painful."

You can have veto power.

Just don't get too comfortable with it. I'll still argue with you out of principle.

choices.choiceText: I'll exercise that veto power every single time. Listen to that tape loop...

nodes.partnerDialogue:
Exactly.

You can wander through all these strange chords and build tension, but eventually your ear wants to come home.

I think I spent years avoiding that feeling in my actual life.

Always another gig. Another track. Another room. Something loud enough that I didn't have to sit still.

I don't know if I'm done running around yet.

But talking to you makes staying still sound pretty good.

choices.choiceText: Then stay in the home key with me. We don't need dissonance anymore.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*soft sniffle, then a little laugh*

Okay.

I'm going to remember you said that.

Not because I need some giant promise right now.

I just like the idea that one day I might wake up early and actually expect somebody to be there instead of reaching for my phone out of habit.

choices.choiceText: Hold me to it. I'm counting on it.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
Thank you.

I think I was scared to let anyone hear this because it's not the version of me people know.

No big bass drop. No crowd. No jokes every thirty seconds.

Just me, an old guitar, and a recording I made because I missed my dad.

It feels really personal.

I'm glad you heard it.

choices.choiceText: Tenderness is the highest form of mastery, Trixie.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
Oh wow.

Yeah.

That's exactly what it feels like.

He used to play this progression while my mom made pancakes. I can still remember the kitchen light and the smell of coffee.

I haven't thought about that morning in years.

And now it's five in the morning and somehow it feels like I'm back there for a minute.

choices.choiceText: Then this Sunday, you and me are continuing that tradition.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
I believe you.

And that's the part I'm still getting used to.

I spend so much time around people who are always looking for the next thing that I forgot how good it feels when somebody isn't rushing you toward the next thing.

I don't need some huge promise.

I just want something that gets the chance to become real.

choices.choiceText: Tell me about Sunday morning. Walk me through our date.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
Listen.

There.

That little sound underneath the guitar?

That's his hand hitting the body of the guitar. I could have edited it out, but I left it there.

It's tiny, but that's my favorite part.

You can hear that he was actually sitting there playing it.

It makes the recording feel like a memory instead of just a song.

choices.choiceText: It's timeless. And so is this moment right now.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
Sunday morning.

Nine o'clock.

I'll have my hair down, no stage makeup, and probably that oversized hoodie you've already heard too much about.

I'll make eggs, cut the sourdough, put the coffee stuff on the table, and try not to burn anything because apparently I'm capable of blowing a power supply but still somehow nervous about breakfast.

And honestly?

I'm more excited about you sitting across from me than I am about showing you my gear.

choices.choiceText: I'll bring freshly roasted coffee beans and a hand grinder. It's a date.
Sourdough, farm eggs, and zero volume with the girl of my dreams. Done.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*the cassette reel reaches the end and clicks softly*

The tape's finished.

The sun is fully up now.

I thought I'd feel wrecked after last night, but I actually feel... calm.

I'm going to sleep for a few hours.

And when I wake up, I'm probably going to think about Sunday first.

That's a pretty nice thing to fall asleep thinking about.

choices.choiceText: Sleep gently, my bass queen. Sunday is ours.
Rest those ears and dream in warm frequencies, Trixie.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*sleepy laugh, voice barely above a whisper*

Okay.

Sunday.

No club. No crowd. No pretending to be louder or crazier than I actually feel.

Just breakfast, coffee, and seeing what happens when we have nowhere else we need to be.

Goodnight... or good morning, I guess, {PlayerName}.

And seriously, thank you for staying when things got ugly.

I won't forget that.

choices.choiceText: [Hang Up and Return to Chat]
